newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ rates end sharply higher to offset plunging NZD.
newsitem.headline: NZ rates end sharply higher to offset plunging NZD.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (SEP) 92.26 (PREV 92.84) 90-DAYS 8.60 (PREV 7.70) 3-YR BONDS (SEP) 93.05 (PREV 93.09) 02/01 6.98 (PREV 6.70)
OVERNIGHT CASH 8.60 PCT (PREV 8.05) US 5-YR 6.12 (PREV 6.09) NZD/USD 0.6493/00 (PREV 0.6598/05) US 10-YR 6.21 (PREV 6.19)
New Zealand's key 90-day bank bill rate shot 90 basis points higher to close at 8.60 percent on Friday after the Kiwi dollar plummeted over one U.S. cent.
The sell-off was at its most fierce in the short-end but infiltrated the entire yield curve, the long bond yield rising 22 points to 6.84 percent.
Rates rose to offset the effect of the weaker currency on monetary conditions.

The Monetary Conditions Index, which measures the mix of the exchange rate and the 90-day rate, opened over 100 points below the Reserve Bank's desired level of 825 in the September quarter, reflecting the sharp decline in the currency overnight.
However, the drastic rise in rates brought the MCI back into line and it closed at 772 -- just three points outside the RB's 50-point comfort zone.
Dealers said afternoon trade had settled into a nervous lull but the overwhelming fear was that the Kiwi would resume its downward spiral tonight.
"There's been a few investors around this afternoon, but it's still pretty well offered and I think people are worried about another sell-off in the Kiwi," said one.
He said bill rates would keep rising if the Kiwi continued to fall.
"I suppose in a way they've got to. With the MCI the big focus at the moment, people regard it as being pretty important.
"People have just been worried about the MCI -- it's tunnel vision in a way."
The Reserve Bank has twice reprimanded financial markets this month for taking overall conditions too low on the MCI.
Dealers said the bond market had tried to stave off the selling frenzy but had eventually succumbed.

"Everything is pretty much following the currency. The bonds did try to hold on this morning -- there were a few buyers around this morning in the interbank market -- but since then there's been a lot of selling in the shorter-dated bonds especially, and the rest of the bonds have followed through with that in mind," said one dealer.
He said people were starting to get worried about the situation.
"Yes they are. There's been a bit of activity in the options, with corporates coming in and taking a bit of cover in the short end. But people are pretty concerned.

"I think banks will lift mortgage rates pretty quickly, it's just a matter of when the first one starts. People are pretty nervous, they don't think the slide in the currency is over yet at all," he added.
-- Matthew Brockett, Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 471-4272
